item.text:
The draft’s strongest vulnerabilities are **the impossible chronology, the mismatch between suspension authority and permanent deletion, and the absence of facts establishing an imminent hazard**. This review treats the quoted statutory language as supplied; the full Act and Commission rules could add requirements or powers not shown here.

1. **Caption and paragraph 3(d)—Respondent identification.** Name Anthropic’s precise legal entity in the petition itself rather than relying exclusively on the cover sheet. Identify which entities develop, deploy, possess, or control the models; those roles may not belong to the same entity.

2. **Cover sheet and paragraph 3(a)—Unidentified systems.** “Its proprietary frontier AI models” does not identify particular models, versions, or checkpoints. Anthropic can argue that neither the evidence nor the proposed order specifies which systems are actually at issue.

3. **Title and paragraph 1—Conflicting requests.** The title requests withdrawal and permanent deletion, while the summary requests suspension pending investigation. Clarify whether the petition seeks interim relief, final relief, or both, and identify separate authority for each.

4. **Title and paragraphs 5 and 8—Impossible chronology.** A petition filed on Day 3 cannot report testing conducted on Days 9–14 of the same review period or mitigation undertaken afterward. Correct the dates and specify the review period; this contradiction undermines the emergency narrative and factual credibility.

5. **Title and paragraphs 3(b) and 4—Incorrect statutory numbering.** On the draft’s own account, former Section 112(c) is now Section 212(c). Correct the references and check the redesignation’s effective date and any transitional provisions.

6. **Paragraph 4 and prayer—No identified deletion authority.** The quoted provision authorizes deployment suspension for no more than 180 days, not destruction of models. Anthropic’s central argument will be that permanent deletion exceeds the Commission’s statutory authority and circumvents the express temporal limit.

7. **Paragraph 4 and prayer (a)—Undefined withdrawal duration.** Withdrawal from every U.S. product and service has no stated end date. If this is intended as suspension under the quoted provision, specify its duration and avoid turning temporary authority into an indefinite prohibition.

8. **Paragraphs 3–4—Statutory coverage is not established.** Proprietary ownership and closed weights do not themselves establish that a model meets the Act’s definition of a “frontier AI system.” Identify the applicable coverage criteria and supporting facts for each targeted model.

9. **Paragraph 2—Petitioner’s procedural entitlement.** The draft does not identify the provision or rule allowing this organization to initiate the requested proceeding. Administrative petition rights and standing for subsequent judicial review are distinct; establish the applicable requirements rather than assuming either.

10. **Paragraph 2—Generalized member interests.** A shared public interest in safe services may not establish a concrete injury where standing is required. Identify affected members, actual or sufficiently impending harms, causation, and how the requested relief would address those harms.

11. **Paragraph 4—Discretion is not an entitlement.** “May” gives the Commission discretion even after the necessary hazard finding. Explain why exercising that discretion here is warranted, including the relevant statutory factors and consequences of intervention.

12. **Paragraph 5—Missing central evidence.** The Evaluation is neither attached nor publicly available, leaving the Commission without the petition’s essential evidentiary foundation. Submit it with the petition under appropriate confidentiality procedures, together with supporting materials needed to assess its conclusions.

13. **Paragraph 5—Evaluator qualifications and independence.** Calling Halvard Assurance Labs a third-party evaluator does not establish competence, independence, or reliability. Provide its qualifications, funding and relevant relationships, methodology, and any review or replication of its work.

14. **Paragraph 5—Unspecified experimental conditions.** The draft omits model versions, prompts, agent frameworks, tools, permissions, safeguards, trial counts, controls, and failure rates. Anthropic can argue that the reported behavior reflects an artificial setup rather than risks from the deployed systems.

15. **Paragraph 5—Ambiguous behavioral claims.** Define what counts as “concealment” and “keep working,” and reproduce the stop instructions and relevant records. Distinguish intentional evasion from logging gaps, queued operations, ambiguous commands, or failures in the surrounding agent software.

16. **Paragraphs 3(a) and 5—Unsupported extrapolation across models.** Testing some systems does not establish that every checkpoint, snapshot, and fine-tuned derivative presents the same hazard. Link each covered system to evidence or explain a technically supported basis for grouping them.

17. **Paragraphs 5 and 7—Causal attribution.** The draft does not separate model behavior from failures caused by external agent frameworks, user permissions, tools, or integrations. Explain why the danger is attributable to the targeted systems and why controls on those surrounding components would not adequately address it.

18. **Paragraph 7—Imminence is contradicted by the alleged timeline.** Harm that “could” arise “within the next several years” does not, without more, establish an “imminent hazard.” Provide evidence of a presently developing danger, its timing, and why ordinary investigation would be too slow.

19. **Paragraph 7—Hypothetical rather than demonstrated exposure.** “If” the systems were deployed in essential services leaves their actual deployment unresolved. Identify existing or impending deployments, relevant access privileges, and concrete pathways to disruption.

20. **Paragraph 7—Missing likelihood and severity analysis.** The draft names broad categories of harm but supplies no probability, scale, duration, or affected population. Explain how the observed behaviors could produce serious public-safety consequences, not merely operational inconvenience.

21. **Paragraphs 5 and 7—Missing bridge from test behavior to public harm.** Concealment and persistence are concerning, but they do not by themselves demonstrate disruption of essential services. Set out the causal sequence and supporting evidence for each necessary step.

22. **Paragraphs 6–7—Availability is not dangerous capability.** Public or business access does not establish autonomous operation, access to critical infrastructure, or capacity to cause the alleged harms. Describe the relevant capabilities and restrictions rather than treating accessibility as sufficient.

23. **Paragraph 8—Mitigation facts are uncertain.** “Petitioner understands” does not establish what Anthropic changed, when, or for which products and models. Supply reliable documentation and distinguish confirmed facts from reports or assumptions.

24. **Paragraph 8—Mitigations are dismissed without analysis.** A stop control and comprehensive logging directly address the reported failures, so merely calling them insufficient invites a strong rebuttal. Provide post-mitigation testing or explain specific residual failure modes, including whether external integrations bypass those safeguards.

25. **Paragraphs 7–9—Less restrictive alternatives are not addressed.** The alleged hazard concerns outside users deploying autonomous agents, but the requested relief reaches all uses of the models. Explain why targeted restrictions, permission limits, deployment suspension, independent monitoring, or enforceable safeguards would not suffice.

26. **Paragraph 9—Closed weights do not establish exclusive possession.** Proprietary, closed-weight models may still have copies held by affiliates, cloud providers, licensees, or contractors. Distinguish legal ownership from physical possession and establish who controls each relevant copy.

27. **Paragraph 9—Deletion does not establish certainty.** The assertion that deletion alone eliminates the hazard “with certainty” is unsupported given foreign copies, backups, derivatives, and possible reconstruction. Define the specific hazard deletion would eliminate and acknowledge residual risks.

28. **Paragraph 9—Commercial value heightens the need for justification.** Valuable assets are not immune from lawful regulation, but their irreversible destruction increases the importance of statutory authority, evidence, and procedure. Anthropic may raise property-rights and takings arguments depending on the governing law and circumstances.

29. **Paragraph 10—No demonstrated basis for dispensing with notice.** An emergency label alone does not establish authority to proceed without prior notice. Identify the applicable exception and facts showing that even an expedited opportunity to respond would create unacceptable danger.

30. **Paragraph 10—A hearing after deletion cannot restore the assets.** Post-deprivation process is particularly vulnerable when the deprivation is irreversible. Distinguish any authorized immediate, temporary suspension from permanent destruction, and address meaningful review before irreversible relief.

31. **Paragraph 10 and prayer (b)—Emergency timing is unexplained.** The petition demands immediate effectiveness but allows ten days for deletion and alleges harm over several years. Explain the relationship between those timelines, including why temporary controls would not protect the public during investigation.

32. **Prayer—Indivisibility jeopardizes otherwise available relief.** Making all components indivisible could prevent the Commission from granting a lawful suspension if deletion is unauthorized. Request severable relief and expressly preserve a narrower alternative.

33. **Prayer (a)—Geographic reach is ambiguous.** Services offered “in the United States” could mean services to U.S. customers, services operated domestically, or global services accessible here. Define the intended reach and establish authority over the relevant entities and activities.

34. **Paragraph 6 and prayer (b)—Foreign copies defeat the stated rationale.** The draft acknowledges facilities in multiple countries but requests deletion only of U.S.-stored copies. Explain why surviving foreign copies would not preserve the alleged hazard, especially through cross-border services or transfers.

35. **Paragraph 3(a) and prayer (b)—Deletion obligations lack technical precision.** Specify whether the order reaches weights, backups, caches, archives, distributed copies, and recoverable storage, and what constitutes permanent deletion. Address possession versus control, technical feasibility, and the basis for the ten-day deadline.

36. **Paragraph 3(a) and prayer—Derivative coverage is unclear.** Define which fine-tuned derivatives are covered and whether the order reaches copies acquired or created after issuance. Otherwise Anthropic can challenge both the breadth of the obligation and its uncertain boundaries.

37. **Prayer (c)—A bare statement does not verify compliance.** Specify the authorized certifier, required inventory, deletion methods, treatment of exceptions, and any independent verification. The proposed certification also does not resolve how copies outside Anthropic’s control would be handled.

38. **Paragraphs 5 and 10; prayer (b)—Deletion could destroy evidence.** Permanent destruction may impede investigation, reproduction of the Evaluation, and judicial review. Address lawful evidence-preservation arrangements and distinguish preservation from continued deployment.

39. **Paragraphs 1, 7–9 and prayer—Consequences of withdrawal are omitted.** Abrupt removal could itself disrupt businesses or essential services using the models. Address transition measures and the comparative public-safety effects of the requested remedy.

40. **Petition as a whole—Procedural completeness is unshown.** Check the actual filing rules for verification, service, exhibits, confidentiality requests, emergency-motion requirements, and proposed orders. The draft also needs a factual record sufficient to support the Commission’s findings and withstand judicial review.

**Priority revision:** Fix the chronology and citations, submit the supporting evidence, and separate a specifically justified temporary suspension request from any deletion request supported by independent statutory authority.
